title: SLO impact messaging and capacity decision matrix
author: Ava Moreno
body:
Purpose

This page defines a single, repeatable pattern that ties SLO degradation signals to (1) customer-facing messaging, (2) internal routing/priority decisions, and (3) capacity and error-budget mitigations. The goal is to remove ambiguity during incidents so engineers and PMs can make consistent, auditable choices under pressure.

Scope

- Applies to all externally facing inference services (hosted API, dedicated endpoints, and private control plane) and their dependent platform services (routing, caching, autoscaler).
- Targets SLO degradations that affect availability (5xx/timeout), latency (p95/p99 tail), and correctness (regressions against a baseline eval).
- Not a substitute for full post-incident review; see Incident Review Standards page for sequencing.

Definitions

- SLO: objective for a customer-observable metric (e.g., request success rate >= 99.95% monthly).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO target over a rolling window.
- Burn rate: how quickly the error budget is being consumed relative to baseline.
- Customer-impact tier: low/medium/high (defined below).

Overview of the pattern

1) Detect: telemetry flags a threshold (quantile/ratio/burn-rate).
2) Classify: map the telemetry to a customer-impact tier using the Decision Matrix.
3) Route: assign incident priority, notify stakeholders, and set owner.
4) Act: run capacity or mitigation playbooks mapped to the tier.
5) Communicate: publish targeted messages (internal and external) using templates.
6) Contain: short-term throttles/fallbacks, then remediate and restore.

Decision Matrix (Telemetry -> Tier -> Action)

This ASCII table shows typical thresholds we use. Individual services may tune thresholds in their SLO contract.

| Telemetry signal | Threshold (example) | Customer-impact tier | Immediate action | Oncall owner | Escalation window |
|------------------|--------------------:|----------------------|------------------|-------------|------------------:|
| 5xx rate         | > 0.5% p10 over 10m | High                 | Route P0, page SRE, run degrade containment | service-oncall | 5m |
| p99 latency      | +300ms over baseline | Medium              | Route P1, notify product, enable latency hedge | service-oncall | 15m |
| error budget burn| > 10x sustained 1h | Medium-High         | Throttle non-critical tenants, open capacity request | capacity-team | 30m |
| correctness regressions | Reg-test failure rate > 2% | High    | Suspend rollout, rollback to pinned version | model-team | 10m |
| cache miss storm | cache-miss rate > 2x baseline | Low-Medium   | Enable degraded cache policy, prune large responses | infra-oncall | 30m |
\nMapping rules and rationale

- High: Customer-visible failures that materially impact availability or correctness for many customers. Require immediate paging and a P0 incident path.
- Medium: Performance degradations and rapid error-budget consumption that may affect SLAs for a subset of customers. Require quick mitigation and capacity adjustments.
- Low: Anomalies with low user-facing impact; treat as tickets or P2 incidents unless they escalate.

Incident routing and message templates

Routing rules (who to page)
- High tier: page primary service oncall + SRE escalation channel + product lead.
- Medium tier: notify primary oncall and send summary to the service channel; the oncall owner decides if escalation is needed.
- Low tier: create an issue and @-mention the steward.

External customer message template (minimal):

Subject: [Redwood] Degraded performance for inference API in region {region}
Body: We are currently investigating increased errors/latency for the Redwood inference API in {region}. Our team has activated mitigation steps and expects the next update within {eta_minutes} minutes. We will follow-up with a full incident report.

Internal incident status template (first 10 minutes):

- Summary: <one-line summary of impact>
- Detection: <signal and time>
- Scope: affected routes/models/regions/tenants
- Customer impact: {low|medium|high} (reason)
- Immediate actions taken: list (eg. rollback, throttle, enable fallback)
- Owner: <name> (oncall)
- Next update: t+{minutes}

Capacity decision matrix (detailed runbook mapping)

When telemetry maps to Medium or High, the oncall should evaluate capacity actions in the following order. Each step includes a guardrail check (safety) and an expected rollback/verification action.

1) Enable admission control for non-critical traffic
   - Guardrail: only allow after verifying headroom >= 10% on healthy clusters.
   - Command (example):

   ```bash
   # Add a deny rule for tenant group:best-effort
   rwctl admission set --tenant-group best-effort --mode deny --reason \"error-budget-protection\"
   ```

   - Verification: monitor headroom metric and p95 latency for 5 minutes.

2) Increase GPU warm pool (if cold-starts observed)
   - Guardrail: ensure quota is available and cost-annotation is set.
   - Command: `k8s scale --replicas=+N deployment/model-warm-pool`

3) Route traffic to a lower-cost compatible model variant (quantized)
   - Guardrail: chosen variant must have a compatibility tag and pass smoke eval.

4) Fallback degrade response (shortened output length / best-effort caching)
   - Guardrail: only if correctness is not impacted; change must be reversible.

5) Emergency reserved capacity request (Dedicated customers only)
   - Process: open capacity ticket to Capacity SRE Pager with timeframe and justification. Estimated lead time: 30–120 minutes depending on region.

Error budget actions and thresholds

- Burn-rate 3x for 1h: engineering notification and weekly postmortem requirement.
- Burn-rate 10x sustained for 30m: immediate medium-tier mitigation (admission control).
- Burn-rate 30x or >50% of budget consumed in 24h: escalate to product and account teams and begin contractual communication prep.

Telemetry contract that each service must publish

Services must maintain an SLO contract page with the following single-line fields and links:
- slo_name (text)
- metric_source (Prometheus job / exporter)
- quantiles_monitored (list, e.g., p50,p95,p99)
- burn_window (e.g., 1h / 24h)
- alert_rules (link to rule ids)
- owner (pager duty name)
- capacity_contacts (list)

Runbook: end-to-end incident example (p95 tail spike during model rollout)

1) t+0: Alert fires: p99 latency > baseline + 350ms (10m window).
2) Classify: Medium tier (performance). Oncall takes ownership.
3) Immediate: Pause rollout, mark model traffic split to 0%.
4) Mitigate: Enable admission control for non-critical tenants and scale warm pool +2 replicas.
5) Monitor: After 7 minutes p95 improves to within 10% of baseline.
6) Communicate: Post internal update and publish external minimal note to status page.
7) Post-incident: Trigger a focused eval against the rolled-back model and update rollout checklist.

Ownership and escalation contacts

- Primary owner: service oncall (specified in SLO contract).
- Secondary: eng-sre escalation team.
- Capacity owner: capacity-sre@redwood.internal.
- Customer comms: customer-success@redwood.internal.

Post-incident expectations and evidence to collect

Every incident routed via this pattern must include the following in the incident record before closure:
- Detection evidence (alert IDs, raw metric snippets).
- Error-budget burn charts for relevant windows.
- Timeline of actions (who did what and when).
- Rollback/mitigation commands and outputs.
- Customer-facing messages sent and delivery receipts.

Examples: alert rule and sample slack snippet

Example Prometheus alert (text snippet):

```
- alert: InferenceP99LatencyHigh
  expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, service)) > (baseline_p99 + 0.35)
  for: 10m
  labels:
    severity: "page"
  annotations:
    summary: "p99 latency elevated for {{ $labels.service }}"
```
\nSample internal Slack message (first update):

@channel: [INCIDENT] Inference p99 spike in us-west-2 (service: text-generation). Owner: Ava Moreno. Impact: medium - increased latency for requests routed to model-v3. Actions: paused rollout, enabled admission control for best-effort tenants, scaling warm pool +2. Next update in 10m.

Governance and review cadence

- Any High-tier incident requires a full postmortem using the company incident template within 72 hours.
- Medium-tier incidents where the error budget exceeded 10% must have a technical retro and a capacity action plan linked to the incident record within 14 days.
- SLO contracts and Decision Matrix thresholds must be reviewed quarterly by service owners and SRE.

Related pages

- Incident Review Standards (link to canonical template)
- SLO contract template and checklist
- Capacity provisioning and quota process

Appendix: decision examples and constraints

- If Dedicated customers are affected and a mitigation reduces performance for Shared customers, prefer tenant isolation (admission control) over global throttles.
- Cost-awareness rule: avoid emergency capacity expansion that increases projected monthly cost > 25% without explicit approval from product finance.

Contact and feedback

If you have suggestions for improving this matrix or need help mapping your service, open a PR on the eng-sre handbook repo and ping the SRE team channel.
